transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Yeah, um… I guess what brings me in is what happened at work. I’m a personal care aide, so we talk about safety stuff all the time, and in this staff meeting I got real worked up about fall prevention. Like, I was trying to show them, but then I was moving chairs around and waving my arms and acting out this whole drill, like someone falling and me catching them or blocking the path or—anyway, people were telling me to sit down, and I knew they were saying it, but I couldn’t really stop right then.

It got embarrassing after. I didn’t mean for it to be a whole thing.
During that meeting, did you feel unusually energized or high?

Yeah… I did. Not like happy exactly, but like bright, you know? Fired up. Like everything I was saying finally made sense and I could see how it all lined up. And then when people were slowing me down or saying, “Sit down,” I got irritated fast—snapped harder than I meant to. I wasn’t trying to be a problem, I just felt like they weren’t getting it.
When this happened, were you sleeping much less than usual without feeling tired?

Yeah, I mean… I wasn’t sleeping much. Like two, maybe three hours, and then I’d be up before it was even light out feeling like, okay, let’s go, I got stuff to figure out.

And it didn’t seem strange to me at the time. I’d be in the kitchen or wherever, making plans while the house was still dark, thinking I was just being productive. Not tired, really. At least not then.
Have you ever had a period lasting at least a couple of weeks when you felt very down or lost interest in things most of the day nearly every day?

I don’t know… a couple weeks like that? I mean, I get down sometimes, sure. Everybody does, right? Like if work is weird or people are looking at you different after a meeting, that can sit on you.

But most of the day, every day… I’m not sure. I don’t really track it like that. Sometimes I’ll stop doing things for a while, but then something else comes up and I’m focused on that. So I guess I don’t know how to answer it exactly.
Have you ever had a time when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day for two weeks or longer?

I’m not sure, honestly. Like, two weeks is a long time when you’re in it, you know? I’ve had days where I felt real low, didn’t want to deal with people, didn’t want to get up and do regular stuff… but then I’ll get distracted by something else, like something going on at work or in the building, and it’s hard for me to say if it was every day.

So… depressed most of the day, nearly every day? I don’t know if I can say that for sure.
Have you ever had a time when you felt depressed nearly every day for at least two weeks?

I mean… I hear what you’re asking, but I still don’t know if I can say it like that. Nearly every day for two weeks… I don’t really keep count that way.

Sometimes I’ll feel down for a stretch, and I’ll be off, you know, not really myself. But then something happens—like at work, or with somebody in the apartment building—and my attention goes over there. So I can’t honestly say, “yes, it was every day for two weeks.” I’m just not sure.
Have you ever had a time when you felt hopeless nearly every day for two weeks or longer?

Hopeless… I don’t know. That word feels kind of big, you know? I’ve had times where I felt like things weren’t going right, like no matter what I did people already had their mind made up about me, but two weeks or longer nearly every day… I can’t really pin it down like that.

Sometimes I’ll be thinking about one thing and it feels heavy, then the next day it’s something else, like work stuff or bills or the way somebody talks to you at the store. So I’m not saying no exactly, I just… I don’t know if I’d call it hopeless every day for two weeks.
Were you hospitalized because of that kind of energized period?

Hospitalized? I don’t… I don’t think so, not for that exactly. I mean, when I get really wound up, people make it a bigger thing than it is sometimes, you know? Like everybody wants to say you’re acting different, but they don’t see what’s going on around you.

But if you mean did I go into the hospital because I was energized like that… I’m not sure how to answer. I don’t remember it being explained to me that way. Hospitals, appointments, paperwork—it all kind of gets mixed together after a while.
During one of those energized times, did you ever hear or see things that other people said were not there?

Yeah… I mean, during those times when I was all fired up, sleeping maybe a couple hours and thinking I could get all these big things going, there were times I’d hear calls that weren’t there. Like I’d think somebody was calling me or trying to get my attention, and then nobody else heard it.

And I was also pretty sure my supervisor was setting traps for me at work. Not like a joke—like really watching how I moved, waiting for me to mess up. Work was a mess anyway, people act like they’re just “checking in,” but they know what they’re doing. So… yeah, I guess that was happening during those stretches.
Have you ever heard those calls or felt people were setting traps for you when you were not in one of those fired-up, high-energy periods?

Yeah… yeah, that did happen when I wasn’t all revved up too. There was a stretch where I was more calm, sleeping more regular, not running around trying to start projects or fix everything at once.

But even then, for a few weeks, I’d still hear my name like somebody called me. And at work I still felt like people were keeping notes on me, like writing things down or watching for mistakes. I mean, jobs do that anyway sometimes, they say it’s “documentation,” you know, like when supervisors act friendly but they’re really tracking stuff. But yeah, that wasn’t only when I was high-energy.
At any time when you were not feeling especially energized or unusually down, did the voices or feeling that people were setting traps for you last for two weeks or longer?

Yeah… I think so. There was this calmer time, like I wasn’t all sped up, wasn’t trying to do ten projects at once, and I wasn’t really down like that either. I was sleeping more normal, going to work, doing the regular stuff.

But for several weeks I still kept hearing my name, like somebody called me from another room or from down the hall. And at work I was still sure people were keeping notes on me, watching what I did, like setting me up to catch mistakes. It went on longer than just a few days… yeah, several weeks.

They also report psychotic symptoms (hearing their name/calls and persecutory beliefs that the supervisor was setting traps/monitoring them). Crucially, these psychotic symptoms persisted for several weeks during a period when the patient was neither manic nor depressed, which supports schizoaffective disorder, manic type, rather than bipolar disorder with psychotic features.
